course.title: Introduction to Psychology
course.about: What do your dreams mean? Do men and women differ in the nature and intensity of their sexual desires? Can apes learn sign language? Why can’t we tickle ourselves? This course tries to answer these questions and many others, providing a comprehensive overview of the scientific study of thought and behavior. It explores topics such as perception, communication, learning, memory, decision-making, religion, persuasion, love, lust, hunger, art, fiction, and dreams. We will look at how these aspects of the mind develop in children, how they differ across people, how they are wired-up in the brain, and how they break down due to illness and injury.

bites.headline: Foundations: This Is Your Brain
bites.body: This lecture introduces students to two broad theories of how the mind relates to the body.
bites.attribution_line: Paul Bloom, Introduction to Psychology (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/introduction-psychology/psyc-110 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Keep this bit
bites.body: Dualism is the ubiquitous and intuitive feeling that our conscious mind is separate from our physical bodies, whereas Materialism is the idea that all of our mental states are caused by physical states of the brain.
bites.attribution_line: Paul Bloom, Introduction to Psychology (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/introduction-psychology/psyc-110 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Foundations: Freud
bites.body: This lecture introduces students to the theories of Sigmund Freud, including a brief biographical description and his contributions to the field of psychology.
bites.attribution_line: Paul Bloom, Introduction to Psychology (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/introduction-psychology/psyc-110 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Keep this bit
bites.body: The limitations of his theories of psychoanalysis are covered in detail, as well as the ways in which his conception of the unconscious mind still operate in mainstream psychology today.
